name: chaiscript
desc: Easy to use embedded scripting language for C++
why: Embedded scripting language for C++ with an unusual niche and a small, obscure following worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: ChaiScript is an embedded scripting language for C++, modelled loosely on ECMAScript/JavaScript but with changes to make it easier to use from C++. A host C++ application creates a ChaiScript engine, registers its own functions with it, and then runs script source either a line at a time with eval(string) or a file at a time with eval_file(fname). Values can be passed back to C++ with a typed call such as chai.eval<double>(...). The library is header-only, so there is no separate build step to link against.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says ChaiScript is 'one of the only embedded scripting language designed from the ground up to directly target C++ and take advantage of modern C++ development techniques, working with the developer how they would expect it to work.'
brief.how_it_works: You include <chaiscript/chaiscript.hpp>, instantiate chaiscript::ChaiScript, and expose C++ functions with chai.add(chaiscript::fun(&my_function), "my_function_name"). The README says the engine keeps type safety between the C++ application and user scripts, and supports callbacks, overloaded functions, class methods and STL containers. By default the standard library loads from a loadable module, with an option to compile it into your code instead.

commands_seen.context: Fetches the vcpkg package manager, one of the two documented ways to install ChaiScript.
Integrates vcpkg with the user's build tooling.

brief.install_notes: The README documents vcpkg as the install route (git clone vcpkg, bootstrap, integrate, install chaiscript). Because it is header-only, you add the ChaiScript include directory to your header search path and include <chaiscript/chaiscript.hpp>. It needs a C++ compiler with C++17 support per the README. The homepage's own claims are different (see caveats). Nothing in the README covers the 'chai' executable that Homebrew lists, and I did not see a standalone interpreter command documented.
brief.standout: It is header-only with no preprocessor or external tools, and it is typed against the host C++ program rather than bridged through a C API. Its niche is embedding a scripting language directly into C++ code, which most embedded scripting options do not target this closely.
brief.status: Appears maintained but not clearly active from what I read. The GitHub README shows Travis, AppVeyor and codecov badges, and the homepage claims 'stable releases since 2009' and that 'No bugfix or feature is made without a corresponding unit test.' I did not find a last-release date or last-commit date in the pages I fetched, so recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: Requirements conflict between sources: the homepage says 'just your C++14 compliant compiler' and lists tested platforms as MSVC2013, clang++ and g++, while the README says it requires C++17 and has been tested with gcc 7 and clang 6 (libcxx). The README's CI badges point to Travis and AppVeyor, which may be stale. The README copyright notice covers 2009-2017 and the badge links look dated. The homepage gave no commands or runnable examples beyond a code snippet. Licensed under BSD, per the README and homepage.

It uses a header-only approach, which makes it easy to integrate with existing projects.

judge.reason: ChaiScript’s type-aware bridge lets scripts call native C++ functions and objects directly, making embedded-language interop worth exploring despite stale-looking documentation.

entry.title: ChaiScript
entry.tldr: A header-only scripting language you embed inside a C++ program, so scripts can call your C++ functions and hand typed values back.
entry.deeper_look:
ChaiScript is a scripting language modelled loosely on ECMAScript, built to live inside a C++ application. The host program creates a `chaiscript::ChaiScript` engine, registers its own functions with it, and then runs script source with `eval(string)` for a line at a time or `eval_file(fname)` for a whole file. Results can come back as real C++ types, for example `chai.eval<double>(...)`.

The README describes it as 'one of the only embedded scripting language designed from the ground up to directly target C++'. Instead of bridging through a C API, it is typed against the host program. It keeps type safety between C++ and scripts, and supports callbacks, overloaded functions, class methods and STL containers.

The library is header-only. You include `<chaiscript/chaiscript.hpp>` and there is no separate library to build or link. The standard library loads from a loadable module by default, or can be compiled into your code.

The idea underneath is a useful one: let a compiled program expose a small, safe surface and let someone else drive it with a script, without recompiling. Reading how ChaiScript maps C++ functions and types into a dynamic language is a good way into how embedding works. The project also publishes a formal EBNF grammar, which makes it a small, readable example of a language definition.
entry.install:
brew install chaiscript

Homebrew lists a `chai` executable, but the README does not document a standalone interpreter. The documented route is vcpkg: `git clone https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg.git`, `./bootstrap-vcpkg.sh`, `./vcpkg integrate install`, `vcpkg install chaiscript`. You need a C++ compiler; the README says C++17.

In your C++ code, registers a C++ function so scripts can call it as my_function_name.
Installs ChaiScript through vcpkg, the README's documented route, so you can include the headers in a project.

entry.whats_unique: It is header-only, needs no preprocessor or external tools, and is typed directly against the host C++ program rather than going through a C API.
entry.caveats: The homepage says C++14 while the README says C++17, the CI badges point to Travis and AppVeyor, and the copyright notice stops at 2017, so how actively it is maintained is unclear.
